title: Sharing a formatter and choosing the year letter

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, why can one `static final DateTimeFormatter` serve every thread, when a shared `SimpleDateFormat` cannot?

options.text: It locks itself while it formats, so the threads take turns
options.says: The page lists synchronizing as an old workaround for SimpleDateFormat that kills concurrency; DateTimeFormatter needs no lock.

options.text: It keeps a separate calendar for each thread that uses it
options.says: A per-thread copy is the page's ThreadLocal workaround for SimpleDateFormat; DateTimeFormatter has no calendar to guard.

options.text: Its state never changes, and withZone returns a new formatter
options.says: The page says it is immutable: once created its state never changes, and withLocale and withZone return new instances.

questions.stem: Per this page, why does a strict date pattern use `uuuu-MM-dd` rather than `yyyy-MM-dd`?

options.text: Under STRICT, yyyy is a year-of-era and needs an era G too
options.says: The page says that with STRICT, yyyy also needs an era G, hence uuuu, the proleptic year.

options.text: Under STRICT, yyyy is a week-based year and not the calendar year
options.says: The page describes y as the year-of-era; the trouble it names under STRICT is the missing era, not a week-based year.

options.text: Under STRICT, yyyy reads only two digits and guesses the century
options.says: The page gives the missing era G as the only reason; yyyy still reads a four-digit year.

concepts: A DateTimeFormatter is immutable, so one static final instance is safe for every thread, and withLocale or withZone return new instances.
y is the year-of-era and u the proleptic year, so a STRICT pattern uses uuuu because yyyy would also need an era.
